tool.name: Grafana
tool.tagline: Dashboards, exploration and alerting on top of your metrics, logs and traces
tool.description: Grafana is an open-source observability front end: it queries data sources such as Prometheus, Loki, PostgreSQL or cloud monitoring services and shows the results as interactive dashboards. Teams use it to watch systems in real time, investigate incidents with logs and traces side by side, and alert on what they see. It is the most common way to visualize Prometheus metrics.

modules.name: Logs, traces and other data sources

glossary.def: In Grafana, a saved connection to a system that holds data, such as a Prometheus server or a database: its address, login details and settings. Panels send their queries through it.
A Grafana page of graphs and numbers (panels) arranged in a grid, all showing the same time range, usually about one system or service.
One box on a Grafana dashboard: one or more queries plus the way their results are drawn, such as a line graph, one big number or a table.
In Grafana, the kind of drawing a panel uses, such as Time series (a line graph), Stat (one big number), Gauge, Table or Heatmap.
Grafana's page for trying queries freely without building a dashboard: pick a data source, type a query, and see the graph and the raw results.
In Grafana, a drop-down (or text box) at the top of a dashboard. Its chosen value is put into every query that mentions $name, so one dashboard can show any service or server.
The control at the top right of a Grafana dashboard that sets the time range every panel shows, such as 'Last 6 hours', and how often it refreshes.
A small database that keeps everything in a single file and needs no separate server program. Grafana uses it by default to store its own dashboards and users.
Grafana Labs' hosted service: Grafana run for you, together with storage for your metrics, logs and traces.
The paid edition of Grafana you run yourself, adding features such as finer-grained permissions, reports and query caching.
Grafana's open-source system for storing and searching log lines, organised by labels much as Prometheus organises metrics.
Loki's query language: a label selector like PromQL's, followed by steps that filter, pick apart and count log lines.
In Loki, all the log lines that share one exact set of labels, such as {app="api", env="prod"}, stored together in time order.
A simple log line format of name=value pairs, such as level=error msg="timeout" duration=2s, easy for both people and programs to read.
Grafana's open-source system for storing traces: records of each request's path through the programs of a system.
Tempo's query language for finding traces by conditions on their spans, such as the service name, the duration or the status code.
A record of one request's whole journey through a system, such as a page load that calls three services, made of timed steps called spans.
One timed step inside a trace, such as one service handling a request or one database call, with its start, duration, parent step and details.
One real example stored next to a metric sample, usually the trace ID of a request that was measured, so a point on a graph can link to that request's trace.
A Loki data source setting that finds a value in each log line, such as a trace ID, and turns it into a link, for example to that trace in Tempo.
In Grafana, a value at which colours change, such as green below 0.01, yellow above it and red above 0.05. Alert rules use thresholds to decide when to fire.
A Grafana setting that shows a value as text, optionally coloured, such as 1 as 'UP' in green and 0 as 'DOWN' in red.
A small, simple line graph without axes, drawn under or behind a number to show its recent trend.
A chart of coloured cells: time runs left to right, value ranges go up the side, and each cell's colour shows how many measurements fell there.
A Grafana visualization that draws each series as a coloured bar along time, one colour per state, such as green for up and red for down.
Grafana's format for query results: a small table with named columns (fields), such as Time and Value, plus the labels it belongs to.
A Grafana step that reshapes query results in the browser before they are drawn, such as merging two queries into one table or renaming columns.
In a table, one line of data, such as one series or one record. On a Grafana dashboard, a row is also a titled band that groups the panels under it and can be folded away.
A Grafana panel stored once and linked into many dashboards; editing it changes it everywhere it is used.
In Grafana, a marker drawn on graphs at a moment or over a stretch of time, such as a new release, with a short text. Alert rules also have annotations: extra text such as a summary.
A clickable link on a value in a Grafana panel, whose address is built from that value's labels and time, such as a detail dashboard for the clicked server.
In Grafana, a link set up once from the results of one data source to a query in another, such as from a log line to its trace. (In statistics: how strongly two things move together.)
The JSON text that fully describes a Grafana dashboard: its panels, queries, variables and settings. Everything you click in the editor ends up in it.
In Grafana, a short fixed identifier of a dashboard, data source or folder, such as api-overview, used in URLs and references. (In Linux, a UID is a user's ID number.)
In Grafana, setting up data sources, dashboards and alerting from files read at startup instead of by clicking. (Generally: setting up the servers or accounts a system needs.)
The tool most teams use to record every change to their project files, with who made it and why, so any earlier version can be seen or restored.
A Grafana feature that keeps dashboards in a git repository: Grafana loads them from it, and edits made in Grafana are saved back as commits or pull requests.
A popular tool for managing services from text files: you describe what should exist, such as Grafana folders and dashboards, and it shows a preview of the changes, then makes them.
HashiCorp Configuration Language: the readable text format that Terraform files are written in.
A small language for generating JSON, with variables and functions. Grafonnet is a Jsonnet library for building Grafana dashboards.
Grafana's tool (Inspect, then Query, in a panel's menu) showing exactly what a panel asked the data source, how long it took and what came back.
Google's four key measures for a service: latency (how long requests take), traffic, errors and saturation (how overloaded it is).
One alert produced by a Grafana alert rule for one series, carrying that series' labels; a rule that matches twelve servers can have twelve instances.
In Grafana Alerting, a named place notifications are sent, such as an email list, a Slack channel or a paging service.
In Grafana Alerting, a rule that matches alert labels, such as team=api, to a contact point, with settings for grouping and repeating. Policies form a tree.
A named set of Grafana alert rules in a folder that are checked together on one timer, such as every minute.
How long an alert rule's condition must stay true before the alert fires, such as 5 minutes, so short blips don't notify anyone.
A temporary mute for alerts matching certain labels, for a fixed time such as during maintenance. The alerts still exist; only their notifications stop.
A repeating schedule, such as weekends or a nightly maintenance window, during which a notification policy holds back notifications.
An alert switching between firing and resolved again and again because a value hovers around its threshold, sending a notification each time.
A Kubernetes object holding ordinary settings or small files as name: value pairs, which programs in the cluster can read.
A helper container running next to the main one in the same Kubernetes pod. Grafana's chart uses one to find dashboards in the cluster and hand them to Grafana.
A popular Helm chart that installs a whole Kubernetes monitoring setup at once: Prometheus, Alertmanager, Grafana, exporters and ready-made dashboards.
A program running in Kubernetes that creates Grafana dashboards, folders and data sources from Kubernetes objects describing them.
A very fast database that keeps its data in memory, often used as a shared cache or to let several servers share small pieces of state.

concepts.name: What Grafana is
concepts.summary: Grafana asks data sources such as Prometheus for data and draws it as dashboards; it stores almost no monitoring data itself.
concepts.why: Knowing that Grafana only asks and draws explains where your data, speed problems and permissions really live.
concepts.body:
Prometheus's own web page draws a graph of one query at a time. **Grafana** is a **web application**, a program you use through your browser, that does much more: it puts dozens of graphs on one page, lets you click through them during an incident, and alerts you when something looks wrong. The data itself lives **elsewhere**; Grafana only asks for it and draws the answer.

Each place Grafana reads from is a **data source**: a saved connection with an address (URL), login details and settings. Prometheus is the most common one. Others hold log lines (**Loki**, Grafana's own log store) or business data in ordinary databases such as PostgreSQL and MySQL, and many cloud services work too.

A **dashboard** is one page of graphs and numbers arranged in a grid, all showing the same time range, such as the last 6 hours. Drop-downs at the top, called **variables**, let you switch which server or service it shows.

A **panel** is one box on a dashboard: one or more PromQL queries plus a **visualization**, the kind of drawing used: a line graph over time, one big number, a gauge, a table.

**Explore** is a page for trying queries freely, without building a dashboard. **Alerting** checks queries on a timer and sends notifications, much like Prometheus's alerting rules.

Grafana stores only its own things (dashboards, users, alert rules) in a small database, by default **SQLite**, a database kept in one file. Your metrics stay in Prometheus. So when a panel is slow, the cause is almost always a slow query in Prometheus, not Grafana.

Grafana is free and open source. Grafana Labs, the company behind it, also sells **Grafana Cloud**, a hosted version that comes with storage for your metrics and logs, and **Grafana Enterprise**, which adds features such as finer-grained permissions and reports.
takeaways: Grafana asks data sources for data and draws it; it doesn't store your metrics
Dashboards contain panels; a panel is queries plus a visualization
Explore is for trying queries without a dashboard

quiz.q: A Grafana panel showing Prometheus data loads slowly. Where is the cause most likely?
options: The PromQL query being worked out by Prometheus
quiz.explain: Grafana only passes queries on; the heavy work of answering them happens in the data source.

concepts.name: Installing Grafana and adding Prometheus
concepts.summary: Install Grafana, log in, and connect a Prometheus data source with the right URL and scrape interval.
concepts.why: Nothing appears in Grafana until a data source is connected correctly, and the URL is the most common mistake.
concepts.body:
Grafana is one server program, like Prometheus. Install it from Grafana's package repository with your Linux package manager (the package is `grafana`; start it with `sudo systemctl start grafana-server`), download the program file, or run the official image `grafana/grafana` with **Docker**. It listens on port **3000**: open `http://localhost:3000`, log in as `admin` / `admin`, and you're asked to choose a new password right away.

Settings live in `grafana.ini` (on Linux, `/etc/grafana/grafana.ini`). Any setting can also be given as an environment variable named `GF_<SECTION>_<KEY>`, such as `GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD`, which wins over the file. Grafana keeps its database and add-ons in `/var/lib/grafana`; that folder is what you back up.

Add Prometheus under **Connections, Data sources, Add new data source, Prometheus**:

- **Prometheus server URL**: the address as seen **from the Grafana server**, not from your browser. If both run on one machine, `http://localhost:9090` works.
- **Scrape interval**: set it to your Prometheus scrape interval, such as 15s. Grafana uses it to choose safe windows for `rate()`.
- Login settings, only if your Prometheus asks for a password.

**Save & test** runs a test query. Queries are sent by the Grafana server itself, not by people's browsers, so Prometheus only has to be reachable from Grafana.

One classic mistake with Docker. Docker runs each program in a **container**, a sealed-off box with its own network address. Inside the Grafana container, `localhost` means that container itself, not your machine, so `http://localhost:9090` finds nothing. Use the name of the Prometheus container instead, such as `http://prometheus:9090`, as in the example.
concepts.code:
# docker-compose.yml: runs Prometheus and Grafana as two containers
services:
  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:v3.13.4
    ports: ["9090:9090"]
  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:13.2.0
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
    environment:
      GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD: change-me      # instead of admin/admin
    volumes:
      - grafana-data:/var/lib/grafana          # keep Grafana's data on restart
volumes:
  grafana-data: {}
# In Grafana: Connections > Data sources > Prometheus
#   URL: http://prometheus:9090    (container name, not localhost)
#   Scrape interval: 15s
# Save & test -> "Successfully queried the Prometheus API."
takeaways: Grafana listens on port 3000; settings come from grafana.ini or GF_ environment variables
A data source URL is reached from the Grafana server, not from your browser
Set the data source's scrape interval to match Prometheus
pitfalls: Using http://localhost:9090 when Grafana runs in a Docker container; there it points at the Grafana container itself.

quiz.q: Grafana and Prometheus run as two Docker containers started together, and the Prometheus one is named prometheus. Which data source URL works?
options: Only the machine's public IP address
quiz.explain: Containers started together like this reach each other by name; localhost would be the Grafana container itself.

concepts.name: Your first dashboard and panels
concepts.summary: Create a dashboard, add time series and stat panels with PromQL queries, set legends and the time range, and save it.
concepts.why: Dashboards are what most people use Grafana for, and a few good habits make them readable from day one.
concepts.body:
Create a dashboard with **Dashboards, New, New dashboard, Add visualization**, and pick the data source. The panel editor has three areas: a preview of the panel, the **query** section below it, and the panel's options on the right.

For Prometheus the query editor has a **Builder** mode, where you pick a metric, labels and operations from lists, and a **Code** mode for typing PromQL. Useful options under the query:

- **Legend**: `{{instance}}` or `{{status}}` names each series by one label instead of its full list of labels.
- **Type**: range, instant or both. A range query gives the points for a graph; an instant query gives one value per series, which is what one-number and table panels usually need.

Common visualizations: **Time series** for a line graph over time, **Stat** for one big number with a small trend line under it (a **sparkline**), **Gauge** and **Bar gauge** for values against a limit, **Table** for lists, and **Heatmap** for how histogram measurements are spread out.

The dashboard's **time picker** (top right) sets the range for every panel, such as "Last 6 hours", and how often to refresh. Drag panels to arrange them, and group them under collapsible **rows**: titled bands you can fold away.

Save the dashboard into a **folder** with a meaningful name. Each save keeps a version you can compare and restore later under **Settings, Versions**.

Start small, with the few numbers that answer "is the service healthy?": how many requests it gets, how many fail, and how long they take (its **latency**, the wait between asking and getting an answer). Leave the rest of your metrics for later.
concepts.code:
# $__rate_interval: a safe rate() window Grafana works out for you (a later lesson explains it)

# Panel 1: Time series "Requests per second", legend {{status}}
sum by (status) (rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[$__rate_interval]))

# Panel 2: Stat "Error ratio", unit Percent (0.0-1.0), instant query
# status=~"5.." keeps status codes matching the pattern 5.. (a 5, then any two characters:
# 500, 503...), the server errors; failed requests divided by all requests = share that fail
sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api", status=~"5.."}[5m]))
  / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[5m]))

# Panel 3: Time series "p95 latency", unit seconds
# p95 latency: 95% of requests finished faster than this (the 95th percentile)
# histogram_quantile(0.95, ...) estimates it from the histogram's buckets; le is each bucket's upper limit
histogram_quantile(0.95,
  sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="api"}[$__rate_interval])))

# Panel 4: Stat "Targets up", instant query
sum(up{job="api"})
takeaways: Panel = query + visualization + options
Name series with legends like {{status}}; use instant queries for one-number panels
Save into folders; every save is a version you can restore
pitfalls: One dashboard with 60 panels of every metric; nobody can read it during an incident.

quiz.q: Which visualization best shows the current error ratio as one large number?
quiz.explain: Stat shows a single value, optionally with a sparkline and colours.

concepts.name: Time range, zoom and auto-refresh
concepts.summary: Use the time picker's relative and absolute ranges, zoom into graphs, share links with the range, and set auto-refresh sensibly.
concepts.why: Every panel on a dashboard is driven by the time range; knowing how to move around in time is the basic investigation skill.
concepts.body:
The **time picker** (top right) sets one time range for the whole dashboard. You can type ranges in a short relative form: `now-6h` to `now` is the last six hours, `now/d` rounds down to the start of today, and `now-1d/d` to `now-1d/d` is all of yesterday. You can also type exact dates and times, or pick them on a calendar.

Times are shown in a **time zone** chosen in the picker: your browser's, **UTC** (the world's standard time, with no daylight saving), or a named zone such as Europe/Berlin. It's saved with the dashboard; teams spread across countries often pick UTC.

Moving around:

- **Drag** across a time series panel to zoom into that stretch of time; the whole dashboard follows.
- The **zoom out** button (or `t` then `z`) doubles the range; the arrows (`t` then left or right) shift the window.
- The range is part of the page's URL, as `from=now-6h&to=now` or as Unix timestamps in milliseconds, so a copied link reproduces exactly what you see. The **Share** menu can turn the range into fixed times, so the link still shows the same moment later.

The **refresh picker** next to it re-runs every query every 5s, 10s, 30s, 1m and so on. Admins can limit the choices and set a minimum with `min_refresh_interval` in `grafana.ini`. Each refresh is real work for the data source: a wall-screen dashboard refreshing every 5 seconds keeps Prometheus busy.

In **Dashboard settings** you can hide the picker, save the current range as the dashboard's default, and set a **now delay**: shift "now" back by, say, 1m, so the last point, whose data is still arriving, isn't drawn as a sudden drop.

A single panel can differ from the dashboard with **relative time** and **time shift** in its query options, for example "last 24h, shifted 7d" to show the same graph one week earlier.
concepts.code:
# Relative ranges (from -> to)
# now-6h      now        last 6 hours
# now-7d      now        last 7 days
# now/d       now/d      today (00:00 to 23:59:59)
# now-1d/d    now-1d/d   yesterday
# now/w       now        this week so far
# now-1M/M    now-1M/M   previous calendar month

# The range travels in the URL:
# https://grafana.example.com/d/abc123/api?from=now-6h&to=now&timezone=utc
# fixed times, as Unix timestamps in milliseconds:
# https://grafana.example.com/d/abc123/api?from=1760680800000&to=1760702400000

# grafana.ini: no dashboard may refresh faster than every 10s
[dashboards]
min_refresh_interval = 10s
takeaways: now-6h, now/d and now-1d/d are the relative range forms
Drag on a graph to zoom; the range is in the URL, so links reproduce the view
Auto-refresh is load on the data source; a now delay hides the incomplete last point
pitfalls: Sharing a link with from=now-1h during an incident; by the time someone opens it the interesting hour has scrolled away.

quiz.q: Which range shows all of yesterday, from midnight to midnight?
quiz.explain: /d rounds to day boundaries; now-1d/d as both ends is the whole previous day.

concepts.name: Explore: ad-hoc queries and split view
concepts.summary: Use Explore to try PromQL without a dashboard: the metrics browser, Builder and Code modes, split view, query history and "Add to dashboard".
concepts.why: Most queries start as an experiment; Explore is where you find the right expression before it earns a place on a dashboard.
concepts.body:
**Explore** (the compass icon in the menu) is a scratchpad: choose a data source, write a query, run it, and see a graph plus a table of the raw series, with nothing to save. It has the same controls as a dashboard: a **time picker** at the top right for the time range, and the same query editor.

For Prometheus:

- The **Metrics browser** (in Code mode) lists metric names and, after you pick one, its label names and values, so you can see what is actually scraped before writing anything.
- **Builder** mode puts a query together from lists: a metric, label filters and operations such as rate and sum by. **Code** mode is plain PromQL, with suggestions as you type and an **Explain** switch that describes each step in words.
- **Options** below the query: range or instant type, the legend (how series are named), the smallest step between points, and **Format** (time series, table or heatmap).

**Split view** opens a second Explore pane next to the first, with its own data source, sharing the time range unless you unlink them (the link icon). The classic use is a Prometheus graph on the left and the matching log lines from Loki on the right. Everything is stored in the page's URL, so an Explore link can be shared.

**Query history** keeps every query you ran; star the useful ones and add comments. The **query inspector** shows the exact request sent, the answer and how long it took. When a query is right, **Add to dashboard** turns it into a panel on a new or existing dashboard.

Whether viewers may use Explore depends on their role. On busy live systems admins sometimes switch it off for them, because a query with no filter, such as `{__name__=~".+"}` (every series there is), can overwhelm Prometheus.
concepts.code:
# A typical Explore session, Prometheus data source, Code mode

# 1. Discover: what does the api job expose? (metrics browser, or:)
{job="api"}                              # instant query, lists every series

# 2. Narrow down
rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[5m])

# 3. Shape it, check the legend
sum by (status) (rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[$__rate_interval]))

# 4. Split view: right pane -> Loki, same time range
{app="api"} |= "error"

# 5. Add to dashboard -> panel in "API overview"
takeaways: Explore runs queries without a dashboard; Builder, Code and the Metrics browser help you find them
Split view puts two data sources side by side on one time range
Query history and Add to dashboard turn experiments into panels
pitfalls: Running an unfiltered selector over a large range in Explore and taking Prometheus down with you.

quiz.q: You want to see error logs next to a request-rate graph for the same time range. What do you use?
options: Explore split view with Prometheus on one side and Loki on the other
Two browser windows with separate time pickers
quiz.explain: Split view shows two panes with different data sources and a linked time range.

concepts.name: Time series panel, legend and tooltips
concepts.summary: Configure the time series visualization: lines, bars, points, fill and stacking, axes, gaps in data, legend modes with calculations, and tooltips.
concepts.why: Time series is the default visualization and the one you will tune most; its options decide whether a graph is readable at a glance.
concepts.body:
The **Time series** visualization draws every series the query returns against time. Its main groups of options:

**Graph styles**: lines, bars or points; line width; and **interpolation**, how points are joined: straight lines, smooth curves, or steps, which suit values that jump from one level to the next. **Fill opacity** shades the area under each line.

**Stack series**: off, normal or 100%. Stacked series are drawn on top of each other, so the top edge shows their total. That only makes sense when the series add up to something meaningful, like requests split by status code; never stack latencies.

**Gaps**: when there is no data for a while, Grafana leaves a gap in the line, which is usually what you want, because it reveals failed scrapes. A missing value is called **null**; **Connect null values** draws the line across such gaps instead.

**Axis**: left or right placement, soft min and max (the axis still grows if the data goes beyond them), and log scale. An **override**, a setting that replaces the panel's default for chosen series only, can put one series on a right-hand axis, for example a request count next to a latency.

**Thresholds** are lines or shaded areas at chosen values, such as your target maximum response time, so everyone can see at a glance when a graph crosses one.

The **legend** has a mode (list, table, hidden), a placement (bottom, right) and **values**: calculations such as Last, Max, Mean and Total added for each series, sortable in table mode. Clicking a series name shows only that series; Ctrl/Cmd-click adds more. The names come from the query's legend setting, such as `{{instance}}`.

The **tooltip**, the box that appears when you hover, shows a single series, all series, or nothing; with all you can sort by value, handy with many series. The dashboard-wide **Graph tooltip** setting (Settings, General) adds a shared crosshair: hovering one graph marks the same moment on every panel.
takeaways: Stack only series that add up; keep gaps for missing data
Legend table mode with Last/Max/Mean turns a graph into a summary
A shared crosshair lines up the hovered moment across all panels
pitfalls: Switching on Connect null values everywhere, which hides failed scrapes and outages behind smooth lines.

quiz.q: Which series are safe to stack in a time series panel?
options: Requests per second split by status code
CPU usage of two unrelated clusters as percentages
Any series, stacking is purely cosmetic
quiz.explain: Stacking shows parts of a whole; status-code request rates sum to total traffic, latencies and percentages don't.

concepts.name: Units, thresholds, value mappings and overrides
concepts.summary: Make panels readable with units, decimals, colours that change at set values, text for special values, and per-series settings.
concepts.why: A correctly labelled number with a clear colour beats a raw number that everyone has to interpret.
concepts.body:
The options on the right of the panel editor come in two kinds.

**Panel options** describe the panel itself: title, description and links, plus settings that belong to its visualization, such as line width or stacking.

**Field options** apply to the numbers being shown. (Grafana calls each column of query results a **field**: the time, the value, each label.)

**Unit**: seconds, bytes, percent (0-100) or percent (0.0-1.0), requests per second and many more. Grafana then scales values for you: 0.25 s shows as 250 ms, and 1536 bytes as 1.50 KiB (a **kilobyte** is about a thousand bytes). **Min / Max** and **Decimals** sit next to it.

**Thresholds** are the values where colours change: a base colour plus steps, such as green, yellow above 0.01, red above 0.05. Stat and gauge panels colour themselves with them; time series can draw them as lines or shaded areas.

**Value mappings** turn values into text: `1` into "UP" and `0` into "DOWN", or a range of values into a word. **Data links** make values clickable, opening an address built from the value and its labels, such as a more detailed dashboard.

**Overrides** change field options for chosen series only, picked by name, by regular expression, by query or by type. An override replaces the panel's default for those series: a different unit for one series, a dashed line for "last week", a fixed red for errors.

Set units in Grafana rather than multiplying in PromQL, so values stay correct and readable at every scale.
takeaways: Set the unit and let Grafana scale values
Thresholds colour values; value mappings turn values into text
Overrides change options for selected series only
pitfalls: Choosing percent (0-100) for a ratio between 0 and 1, so 5% shows as 0.05%.

quiz.q: Your query returns 0.0312 for a ratio. Which unit shows it as 3.12%?
quiz.explain: Percent (0.0-1.0), called percentunit in JSON, multiplies the ratio by 100 for display.

concepts.name: Stat, gauge and bar gauge
concepts.summary: Show single values well: the reduce calculation, colour and graph modes of Stat, min/max and markers for Gauge, and Bar gauge for comparing many values.
concepts.why: The big numbers at the top of a dashboard are what people read first, and a wrong reduce calculation makes them lie.
concepts.body:
All three visualizations boil each series down to **one value** and colour it with the thresholds from the field options.

**Calculation** (under Value options) picks how a series becomes one number: Last non-null (the newest real value), `Last *` (the newest value even if it's empty, which Grafana calls **null**), Mean, Max, Min, Total, Count, Difference and more.

Which one? For "current error ratio" from a range query you want Last non-null. For "requests in the selected time range", use an instant query with `increase()` over `$__range`, a built-in value holding the dashboard's whole range. With an **instant** query there is only one value, so the calculation doesn't matter. **Fields** chooses which numeric fields are shown, and **Limit** caps how many series appear.

**Stat** shows the number, optionally with a sparkline (graph mode area) and the series name. Colour mode is none, value, or a coloured background (solid or fading); text mode is auto, value, value and name, or name. Orientation and text size help when there are many numbers. Newer versions can also show the **percent change** since the start of the range.

**Gauge** draws the value on an arc between a **min** and a **max**, with the thresholds marked around it. Set min and max yourself, otherwise Grafana guesses them from the data. Use it for things with a natural limit: disk space, memory, how full a list of waiting jobs is.

**Bar gauge** draws one bar per series, horizontal or vertical, all on one shared scale, with sorting. It is the right choice for "top 10 programs by memory" or the fill level of many disks.
concepts.code:
# Stat: Error ratio (instant query, unit percentunit, thresholds green/orange 0.01/red 0.05)
sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api", status=~"5.."}[5m]))
  / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[5m]))

# Stat: Requests in selected range (instant, calculation irrelevant)
sum(increase(http_requests_total{job="api"}[$__range]))

# Gauge: Disk used, unit percentunit, min 0, max 1
1 - node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/"} / node_filesystem_size_bytes{mountpoint="/"}

# Bar gauge: Memory by job, unit bytes, sort descending, instant
topk(10, sum by (job) (process_resident_memory_bytes))
takeaways: Stat, gauge and bar gauge reduce each series with a calculation; pick Last non-null or use instant queries
Gauges need explicit min and max
Bar gauge compares many series on one scale
pitfalls: Leaving the calculation at Mean for a "current value" stat, so it shows the average of the last 6 hours.

quiz.q: A Stat panel uses a range query and should show the current value. Which calculation is right?
quiz.explain: Last non-null takes the newest real sample; Mean and Total summarise the whole range.

concepts.name: Table panel
concepts.summary: Build readable tables: instant queries in table format, column filters, coloured cells, small gauges and graphs in cells, and footers.
concepts.why: Lists of servers, targets or customers are tables, and a table needs its data in a different shape than a graph does.
concepts.body:
A **Table** shows query results as rows and columns, one column per field. The first thing to get right is the **shape** of the data.

A Prometheus range query returns each series as its own small table of times and values (Grafana calls these **data frames**), and the table panel shows only one at a time, with a picker to switch. What you usually want is one row per series. So set the query **Type** to **instant** and **Format** to **Table**: each label becomes a column, plus `Time` and `Value`.

With several queries, a **transformation**, a step that reshapes results before they're drawn, combines them: **Merge** joins them into one table, and **Organize fields** renames and hides columns. The Transformations lesson covers more.

Useful options:

- **Column filter** adds a filter to each column header. **Pagination** splits a long table into pages, and a **footer** adds totals, means or counts.
- **Column width**, **minimum width** and **cell height**; **align** left, centre or right.

**Cell options**, set per column with overrides, change how cells look: text or background coloured by thresholds, a small gauge inside the cell, a sparkline, or a data link. Value mappings turn `0`/`1` into "down"/"up" with colours, which reads far better than numbers.

Sort by clicking a column header, or permanently with the Sort by transformation. Hide the `Time` column of instant queries: it only holds the moment the query was run.

Tables draw every row the query returned, so keep results short with `topk()`. Thousands of rows make the browser crawl, and nobody reads them anyway.
takeaways: Instant query + Table format gives one row per series
How cells look (coloured background, gauge, sparkline) is set per column with overrides
Keep tables short with topk()
pitfalls: Using a range query in a table and getting a picker of separate frames, each with hundreds of timestamps.

quiz.q: A Prometheus table shows a drop-down of frames instead of one row per instance. What fixes it?
options: Set the query to instant and format Table
quiz.explain: Range queries return a time series per instance; an instant query in table format yields one row each.

concepts.name: Heatmap, state timeline and logs panels
concepts.summary: Draw latency distributions from Prometheus histograms as heatmaps, show discrete states over time with state timeline and status history, and embed logs.
concepts.why: Averages hide the shape of latency and up/down states; these visualizations show distribution and state changes that a line graph can't.
concepts.body:
**Heatmap** shows how a distribution changes over time: the X axis is time, the Y axis the value buckets, and colour the count in each cell. For a Prometheus **histogram**, query the `_bucket` series summed by `le` and set the query **Format** to **Heatmap**: Grafana then sorts the buckets, converts cumulative counts into per-bucket counts and labels the Y axis with the bucket bounds. Native histograms are supported directly. Options cover the colour scheme and scale (exponential works well for latency), Y axis unit, bucket count for raw data, and **Calculate from data**, which sorts plain time series into value ranges itself when the source has no buckets.

**State timeline** shows a few distinct values per series as coloured bars along time: service up or down, which version is running, alert state. Feed it numbers and give them meaning with **value mappings**, which turn values into named, coloured states (1 to "up" in green, 0 to "down" in red), or with thresholds; **Merge equal consecutive values** collapses runs into one bar. **Status history** is the same idea on a periodic grid, one cell per interval, nicer for many series over long ranges.

The **Logs** visualization embeds a Loki (or Elasticsearch) query on a dashboard, with options to show time, wrap lines, prettify JSON, deduplicate and order. Keep the query narrow and pair it with the dashboard variables so logs follow the selected service.

Together with time series these cover most needs; the Grafana catalogue also has Candlestick, Node graph, Geomap, Canvas and Flame graph for specialised data.
concepts.code:
# Heatmap panel: request latency distribution
# Query options -> Format: Heatmap, Type: range
sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="api"}[$__rate_interval]))
# Y axis unit: seconds; colour scale: exponential

# State timeline: target health, value mappings 1 -> UP (green), 0 -> DOWN (red)
# Legend: {{instance}}
max by (instance) (up{job="api"})

# Status history: did the nightly job succeed each day? (0 = failed, 1 = ok)
max_over_time(job_last_run_success{job="etl"}[1d])

# Logs panel (Loki) following the dashboard variable
{app="$service", env="$env"} | json | level="error"
takeaways: Histogram buckets summed by le + Format: Heatmap = latency distribution over time
State timeline needs value mappings to turn numbers into named, coloured states
Logs panel embeds a narrow Loki query that follows the dashboard variables
pitfalls: Forgetting to sum by le, so every instance contributes its own set of buckets and the heatmap is noise.

quiz.q: What must a Prometheus query for a heatmap panel do?
options: Sum the _bucket series by le and use the Heatmap format
quiz.explain: Grafana needs one series per bucket bound (le) to build the Y axis and compute per-bucket counts.

concepts.name: Dashboard variables and templating
concepts.summary: Add drop-down variables from label values, use them in queries with multi-value and All options, and repeat panels per value.
concepts.why: One templated dashboard replaces a copy per service, environment or instance.
concepts.body:
**Variables** appear as drop-downs at the top of a dashboard and are referenced in queries as `$name` (or `${name}`). Create them under **Settings, Variables**. Types include:

- **Query**: values from the data source. For Prometheus: `label_values(up, job)`, `label_values(http_requests_total{job="$job"}, instance)` (variables can depend on each other), or `query_result(...)` for computed lists.
- **Custom**: a fixed comma-separated list.
- **Data source**: switch between, say, several Prometheus servers.
- **Interval**, **Constant** and **Text box**.

With **Multi-value** or **Include All** enabled, a variable can hold several values. Grafana formats them for the data source; in PromQL use the regex matcher: `{job=~"$job"}`. A custom **All value** like `.*` avoids huge regexes when there are many values.

Built-in variables are always available: `$__interval` and `$__rate_interval` (based on the time range and panel width), `$__range` (the dashboard range, e.g. for `increase(x[$__range])`), and `$__dashboard`, `$__user`.

**Repeat** options create one panel, or one row, per selected value: choose the variable in the panel's **Repeat options**. Variable selections are stored in the URL (`?var-job=api`), so links share the exact view.
concepts.code:
# Variable "job"      (Query, Prometheus)
label_values(up, job)
# Variable "instance" (Query, Multi-value, Include All, depends on $job)
label_values(up{job="$job"}, instance)

# Panel query using both; =~ because instance may hold several values
sum by (instance) (
  rate(http_requests_total{job="$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval]))

# Requests during the whole selected time range (Stat panel)
sum(increase(http_requests_total{job="$job"}[$__range]))

# Shareable link with selections:
# /d/abc123/api?var-job=api&var-instance=All&from=now-6h&to=now
takeaways: label_values(metric, label) fills drop-downs from Prometheus
Use =~ with multi-value and All variables
$__rate_interval and $__range are built-in variables
pitfalls: Using job="$job" with a multi-value variable; it needs =~ to match several values.

quiz.q: A multi-value variable $env has prod and staging selected. Which matcher works?
quiz.explain: Grafana renders multiple values as a regex alternation, which needs the =~ matcher.

concepts.name: Transformations
concepts.summary: Reshape query results inside Grafana: join and merge queries, reduce series to rows, rename, filter and calculate fields.
concepts.why: Tables and comparisons often need data shaped differently than the data source returns it.
concepts.body:
**Transformations** (the Transform tab of the panel editor) process query results **after** they return and before visualization. They are applied in order, and the editor can show the output of each step so you can check it.

Frequently used ones:

- **Merge**: combine several queries into one table, matching on common fields such as time and labels. The usual way to build a table with one column per query.
- **Join by field**: put frames side by side, matching rows that share a value in one field, such as `instance` or `Time`.
- **Reduce**: turn each series into a row with calculations (last, mean, max) across the time range; perfect for "per instance summary" tables.
- **Organize fields by name**: rename, reorder and hide columns.
- **Filter data by values**, **Filter fields by name**: drop rows or columns.
- **Add field from calculation**: compute a new column, for example a ratio of two columns or a row total.
- **Group by**, **Sort by**, **Labels to fields** and **Convert field type**.

Transformations run in the **browser** on already-fetched data, so they can't reduce how much data the query returns. When a calculation can be done in the query itself (dividing or summing in PromQL), do it there: it's faster and works the same in alerting. Use transformations for presentation and for combining data from different data sources.
takeaways: Transformations reshape results in the browser, in order
Merge, Join by field, Reduce and Organize fields cover most tables
Prefer doing maths in the query when possible
pitfalls: Fetching huge raw data and filtering with transformations instead of filtering in the query.

quiz.q: You want one table row per instance with columns from two queries. Which transformation combines them?
quiz.explain: Merge combines several query results into one frame by their common fields.

concepts.name: Rows, repeating panels and library panels
concepts.summary: Arrange panels on the 24-column grid, group them in collapsible rows, repeat panels or rows per variable value, and reuse library panels.
concepts.why: One well-laid-out, repeating dashboard replaces dozens of copies that drift apart.
concepts.body:
A dashboard is a **grid 24 units wide**; each panel has a position and size (`gridPos` with `x`, `y`, `w`, `h` in the JSON model) and you drag and resize in edit mode. Put the most important summary panels at the top, details below, and keep panel heights consistent in a row so the eye can scan.

**Rows** are horizontal dividers that group panels and can be **collapsed**; collapsed rows don't run their queries until expanded, which makes big dashboards load fast. Row titles can use variables (`$job overview`).

**Repeat** creates copies per value of a multi-value variable:

- **Repeat panel** by `$instance`, horizontally with a maximum per row, or vertically. Each copy gets the variable bound to one value, so its query `up{instance="$instance"}` is per copy.
- **Repeat row** by `$cluster` repeats a whole row of panels, which is how per-environment or per-region sections are built.

Repeats are created only for the currently selected values; choosing All with fifty instances creates fifty panels and fifty queries, so give such variables a sensible default.

**Library panels** (Dashboards, Library panels) are panels stored once and linked into many dashboards. Edit the library panel and every dashboard using it updates; **Unlink** turns a linked copy back into a normal panel. They are ideal for a standard "service header" row or a legal-text panel that must be identical everywhere, and they carry their own permissions through folders.

Grafana 12 added **dynamic layouts** (automatic grids, tabs, panels shown only when a condition holds), built on a new version of the dashboard format; the grid above remains the default.
concepts.code:
{
  "panels": [
    {"type": "row", "title": "$cluster", "collapsed": false,
     "gridPos": {"x": 0, "y": 0, "w": 24, "h": 1},
     "repeat": "cluster"},
    {"type": "stat", "title": "Up: $instance",
     "gridPos": {"x": 0, "y": 1, "w": 4, "h": 3},
     "repeat": "instance", "repeatDirection": "h", "maxPerRow": 6,
     "targets": [{"refId": "A", "instant": true,
                  "expr": "up{cluster=\"$cluster\", instance=\"$instance\"}"}]},
    {"type": "timeseries", "title": "Latency",
     "gridPos": {"x": 0, "y": 4, "w": 24, "h": 8},
     "libraryPanel": {"uid": "svc-latency", "name": "Service latency"}}
  ]
}
takeaways: 24-column grid; rows group and collapse panels and skip their queries while collapsed
Repeat panels or rows per selected value of a multi-value variable
Library panels are edited once and update everywhere they are linked
pitfalls: Repeating a panel by a variable whose All value expands to hundreds of items.

quiz.q: You need the same "service health" panel on 20 dashboards and want one place to change it. What do you use?
quiz.explain: Library panels are stored once and linked into many dashboards; edits propagate to all of them.

concepts.name: Annotations, dashboard links and data links
concepts.summary: Mark events with manual and query-driven annotations, link dashboards with variables and time range preserved, and make values clickable with data links.
concepts.why: Markers for each new release of your software, and links to more detailed dashboards, are what turn a set of dashboards into a system you can navigate.
concepts.body:
**Annotations** are markers drawn on time-based panels, at a moment (a vertical line) or over a stretch of time (a shaded region), with a short text. The built-in **Annotations & Alerts** query shows annotations stored in Grafana's own database: ones you add by hand (Ctrl/Cmd-click a graph, or drag to mark a region, then type text and tags) and the state changes of alert rules linked to the dashboard.

Under **Settings, Annotations** you can also add annotations from any data source: a Prometheus expression such as a restart counter, a Loki query for lines containing "deploy", or Grafana's own annotations filtered by tag. The tag route is how release markers usually work: the automated job that ships a new version sends a **POST** request (an HTTP request carrying data) to `/api/annotations` with `{"tags": ["deploy","api"], "text": "v2.3.1"}`, and every dashboard filtering on that tag shows it. Annotation queries run on every refresh, so keep them cheap.

**Dashboard links** (Settings, Links) appear at the top: a link to a URL, to a specific dashboard, or a drop-down of all dashboards with certain **tags**. Tick **Include current time range** and **Include current template variable values** so the target opens on the same service and window. **Panel links** do the same in a panel's menu.

**Data links** are attached to values: clicking a point, bar, table cell or stat opens a URL built from the data. Variables available include `${__value.raw}`, `${__value.time}`, `${__field.labels.instance}`, `${__series.name}`, `${__data.fields.pod}`, `${__url_time_range}` and `${__from}`/`${__to}`, plus dashboard variables. A link to another dashboard looks like `/d/pods?var-pod=${__field.labels.pod}&${__url_time_range}`; a link to Explore can carry a prepared query. **Correlations** (under Administration) set up such links once for everyone, from one data source's results to a query in another.
concepts.code:
# Query annotation (Prometheus): process restarts, title/text from labels
changes(process_start_time_seconds{job="api"}[2m]) > 0
# Title: restart  Text: {{instance}}  Tags: restart

# Deploy markers posted by CI (shown by a Grafana annotation query filtered on tag "deploy")
# curl -X POST https://grafana.example.com/api/annotations \
#   -H "Authorization: Bearer $SA_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
#   -d '{"tags":["deploy","api"],"text":"api v2.3.1"}'

# Data link on a "requests by pod" panel -> pod dashboard, same time range
# Title: Open pod
# URL:   /d/pods/pod-detail?var-namespace=$namespace&var-pod=${__field.labels.pod}&${__url_time_range}

# Data link to Explore with Loki logs for the clicked series
# URL:   /explore?left={"datasource":"loki","queries":[{"expr":"{pod=\"${__field.labels.pod}\"}"}],"range":{"from":"${__from}","to":"${__to}"}}
takeaways: Annotations come from Grafana's DB (manual, alerts, API) or from data source queries
Dashboard links can carry the time range and variable values to the target
Data links build URLs from the clicked value's labels and time
pitfalls: A data link to another dashboard without ${__url_time_range}, so it opens on the default range and the spike is gone.

quiz.q: A CI pipeline should mark each deployment on every dashboard of the service. What is the simplest way?
options: Add a text panel listing deployments
POST a tagged annotation to the Grafana API and add a tag-filtered annotation query to the dashboards
Create an alert rule per deployment
quiz.explain: Grafana-stored annotations filtered by tag appear on any dashboard that queries those tags.

concepts.name: Dashboard JSON model, export and versions
concepts.summary: Read a dashboard's JSON model (uid, panels, variables, schemaVersion), export and import it between Grafana servers, and compare and restore versions.
concepts.why: Everything you click in the editor ends up in this JSON; reading it is the step from clicking dashboards together to reviewing, generating and versioning them.
concepts.body:
Every dashboard is one JSON document, its **JSON model**, visible under **Edit, Settings, JSON Model**. The important fields:

- `uid`: the stable identifier used in URLs (`/d/<uid>/<slug>`) and links. `id` is a number from one Grafana server's own database; it is ignored on import and should be `null` (empty) in files.
- `title`, `tags`, `timezone`, `time` (default range), `refresh`, `graphTooltip`.
- `templating.list`: the variables, each with `query`, `datasource`, `multi`, `includeAll`, `current`.
- `annotations.list` and `links`.
- `panels[]`: each with `type`, `gridPos`, `datasource` (`{"type": "prometheus", "uid": "prom-main"}`), `targets` (queries), `fieldConfig.defaults` and `overrides`, `options`, and `transformations`. Rows are panels of type `row` holding collapsed panels.
- `schemaVersion` and `version`: Grafana upgrades dashboards saved in older formats when it loads them, and `version` goes up with every save.

**Export** (Share, Export) offers the raw model or **Export for sharing externally**, which replaces concrete data source UIDs with placeholders like `${DS_PROMETHEUS}` listed under `__inputs`. On **Import** (Dashboards, New, Import) the user maps each input to a local data source, and that is how dashboards from grafana.com/dashboards, where every published dashboard has a numeric id, work across installations.

**Versions** (Settings, Versions) lists every save with author and message, lets you **compare** two versions as a **diff** (the lines removed and added), and **restore** an older one, which creates a new version rather than rewriting history. Dashboards loaded from files (provisioning, a later lesson) keep their history too, but are overwritten from the file.

Grafana 12 added a new version of this format (v2) and a new API for dashboards (`dashboard.grafana.app`), used by the new layouts and by **Git Sync**, which keeps dashboards in a git repository; the classic model above remains supported and is still what most tools produce.
concepts.code:
{
  "uid": "api-overview",
  "id": null,
  "title": "API overview",
  "tags": ["api", "service"],
  "timezone": "browser",
  "schemaVersion": 41,
  "version": 17,
  "time": {"from": "now-6h", "to": "now"},
  "refresh": "1m",
  "graphTooltip": 1,
  "templating": {"list": [{
    "name": "job", "type": "query", "query": "label_values(up, job)",
    "datasource": {"type": "prometheus", "uid": "${DS_PROMETHEUS}"},
    "refresh": 2, "multi": false, "includeAll": false}]},
  "__inputs": [{"name": "DS_PROMETHEUS", "type": "datasource",
                "pluginId": "prometheus", "label": "Prometheus"}],
  "panels": [{
    "id": 1, "type": "timeseries", "title": "Requests",
    "gridPos": {"x": 0, "y": 0, "w": 12, "h": 8},
    "datasource": {"type": "prometheus", "uid": "${DS_PROMETHEUS}"},
    "targets": [{"refId": "A", "expr": "sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=\"$job\"}[$__rate_interval]))"}],
    "fieldConfig": {"defaults": {"unit": "reqps"}, "overrides": []},
    "options": {}
  }]
}
takeaways: uid is stable and used in URLs; id belongs to one server's database and should be null in files
Export for sharing externally replaces data sources with ${DS_*} inputs mapped on import
Versions can be compared as a JSON diff and restored
pitfalls: Copying a dashboard JSON between instances with concrete data source uids that don't exist there, so every panel shows "datasource not found".

quiz.q: What does "Export for sharing externally" change in the JSON?
options: It replaces data source references with ${DS_...} inputs that are mapped on import
It converts the dashboard to the v2 schema
quiz.explain: The __inputs block lets the importer bind each placeholder to a local data source.

concepts.name: Dashboard design: RED, USE, golden signals
concepts.summary: Structure dashboards around RED, USE and the four golden signals, build a drill-down hierarchy, and apply layout conventions that work in incidents.
concepts.why: Most dashboards fail not for lack of data but because nobody can answer "is it broken, and where?" from them in thirty seconds.
concepts.body:
Good dashboards answer a question for an audience. Three well-known checklists tell you which panels belong on them:

- **RED** for request-driven services: **Rate** (requests per second), **Errors** (failed requests per second or error ratio), **Duration** (latency distribution, p50/p95/p99 or a heatmap). One row of RED per service, split by endpoint below.
- **USE** for resources (CPU, memory, disk, network, queues): **Utilization** (how busy), **Saturation** (how much queued or over capacity), **Errors**.
- The **four golden signals** from Google's book on **SRE** (site reliability engineering): latency, traffic, errors and saturation, which is RED plus saturation.

Organise dashboards as a **hierarchy** with links between the levels: an overview with one stat row per service (traffic, error ratio, p95, with thresholds), a per-service dashboard with the RED rows and dependencies, and detail dashboards per instance or database. Data links and tag-based dashboard links let you drill down without losing the time range.

Layout conventions:

- Top-left is the most important thing; summary stats first, time series below, tables and logs last.
- Same unit, colour and Y-axis scale for the same quantity everywhere; green/yellow/red thresholds only where they mean something, taken from your **SLOs** (agreed reliability goals, such as 99.9% of requests succeeding).
- Short titles, a **description** on every non-obvious panel (shown on hover), and legend names that fit.
- One dashboard per audience and purpose; a wall screen, an on-call view and a capacity planning dashboard are different dashboards.

Finally, use **variables** for environment and service so you maintain one dashboard, and keep its JSON model in **git**, the usual tool for tracking changes to files.
concepts.code:
# Service overview row (per $service), RED
# Rate (req/s)
sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="$service"}[$__rate_interval]))
# Error ratio (percentunit, thresholds at SLO: orange 0.1%, red 1%)
sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="$service", status=~"5.."}[$__rate_interval]))
  / sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="$service"}[$__rate_interval]))
# Duration p95 (seconds)
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (
  rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service="$service"}[$__rate_interval])))

# Resource row, USE (CPU)
# Utilization
1 - avg(rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval]))
# Saturation (run queue per core)
node_load1{instance=~"$instance"} / count without (cpu, mode) (node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle", instance=~"$instance"})
takeaways: RED for services, USE for resources, golden signals = RED + saturation
Build a drill-down hierarchy: overview, service, instance, linked with time range preserved
Consistent units, colours and thresholds tied to SLOs
pitfalls: A dashboard that is a dump of every metric the exporter has, instead of the handful that answer "is it healthy?".

quiz.q: Which three panels make up a RED row for an HTTP service?
options: Request rate, error rate, request duration
quiz.explain: RED stands for Rate, Errors and Duration; USE is the resource-oriented counterpart.

concepts.name: SQL data sources and macros
concepts.summary: Chart data from PostgreSQL or MySQL with time-series queries, Grafana's time macros and table formats.
concepts.why: Business numbers such as orders or sign-ups often live in **relational databases**, and Grafana can chart them next to system metrics.
concepts.body:
Grafana ships data sources for PostgreSQL, MySQL and Microsoft SQL Server. These are relational databases: they keep data in tables of rows and columns and are queried in **SQL**, their standard language (`SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ...`). Connect with a **read-only database user**: anyone who can edit a dashboard can run any query the data source allows.

A query can be formatted as a **table** or a **time series**. For time series, return a column named `time` (a timestamp, or a Unix timestamp in seconds), one or more numeric value columns, and optionally a text column called `metric` whose values name the series. Sort by time.

**Macros** are placeholders that Grafana expands into real SQL before sending the query, inserting the dashboard's time range and interval:

- `$__timeFilter(created_at)` becomes a `BETWEEN` condition for the selected range, so the database can use an **index** on that column (a lookup structure, like a book's index) instead of reading every row.
- `$__timeGroupAlias(created_at, $__interval)` buckets timestamps into intervals and aliases the column as `time`.
- `$__timeFrom()` and `$__timeTo()` give the range bounds; `$__unixEpochFilter()` handles timestamps stored as whole numbers of seconds.

Dashboard variables work in SQL too, including query variables like `SELECT DISTINCT country FROM customers`. A multi-value variable is written out as a comma-separated list of quoted values, ready for `IN ($country)`.

Keep queries cheap: always filter with `$__timeFilter`, do the counting and summing in SQL, and point Grafana at a **read replica** (a copy of the database kept for reading) rather than the main database your application writes to.
concepts.code:
-- Orders per interval by country, as a time series panel
SELECT
  $__timeGroupAlias(created_at, $__interval),
  country AS metric,
  count(*) AS orders
FROM orders
WHERE $__timeFilter(created_at)
  AND country IN ($country)          -- multi-value variable
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1;

-- Expands roughly to (PostgreSQL):
-- SELECT floor(extract(epoch from created_at)/60)*60 AS "time", ...
-- WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-10-17T06:00:00Z' AND '2026-10-17T12:00:00Z'
--   AND country IN ('DE','FR')
takeaways: Time series queries return time, value columns and an optional metric column
$__timeFilter and $__timeGroupAlias insert the dashboard's range and interval
Use a read-only user and preferably a read replica
pitfalls: Forgetting $__timeFilter, so every refresh scans the whole table.

quiz.q: What does $__timeFilter(created_at) do?
options: Adds a condition restricting created_at to the dashboard's time range
quiz.explain: It expands to a range condition using the selected from and to times.

concepts.name: Loki and LogQL basics
concepts.summary: Query logs in Loki: stream selectors, line filters, json and logfmt parsers, label filters, line_format, and metric queries that turn logs into graphs.
concepts.why: Loki is the logs half of the Grafana stack, and **LogQL** is how you go from "something is wrong" to the lines that say what.
concepts.body:
**Loki** stores log lines in **streams**: all the lines that share one exact set of labels (`app`, `env`, `host`, `level`) are kept together in time order. Loki **indexes** only those labels, meaning it keeps a quick lookup for them, not for the text of the lines. That is why it is cheap, and why values with very many possibilities, such as user or request IDs, must stay inside the line (or in structured metadata, extra data stored with each line), not become labels.

A **LogQL** query is a pipeline, read left to right:

- **Stream selector**: `{app="api", env="prod"}`, with `=`, `!=`, `=~`, `!~` like PromQL. At least one non-empty matcher is required.
- **Line filters**: `|= "error"` contains, `!= "healthz"` does not contain, `|~ "timeout|refused"` regex, `!~` not regex. They are fast; put them first.
- **Parsers** pick each line apart into named values (fields): `| json`, `| logfmt`, `| pattern "<ip> - <_> <method> <path>"`, `| regexp "..."`.
- **Label filters** on extracted fields: `| status >= 500`, `| duration > 2s`, `| method="POST"`.
- **Formatting**: `| line_format "{{.method}} {{.path}} {{.duration}}"` rewrites the line, `| label_format` renames labels, `| drop`/`| keep` trim fields.

**Metric queries** wrap a log query in a range function and add up the results like PromQL: `count_over_time({app="api"} |= "error" [5m])` counts lines, `rate(...)` per second, `bytes_rate` bytes per second, and `sum by (status) (...)` groups. With `| unwrap duration` you can compute `quantile_over_time(0.95, ... [5m]) by (path)` from values in the logs. These queries draw graphs and can feed alert rules.

In Explore, the **log volume** histogram above the lines shows counts by level, the **Logs** app (Logs Drilldown) offers a query-less browsing view, and clicking a label value adds it to the selector.
concepts.code:
# Streams of the API in prod, lines containing "error" but not health checks
{app="api", env="prod"} |= "error" != "/healthz"

# Parse JSON logs, keep slow 5xx responses, reshape the line
{app="api"} | json | status >= 500 | duration > 1s
  | line_format "{{.method}} {{.path}} {{.status}} {{.duration}}"

# logfmt lines (level=error msg="..." ) from one namespace
{namespace="payments"} | logfmt | level="error"

# Metric query: error lines per second, by app
sum by (app) (rate({env="prod"} |= "error" [5m]))

# p95 request duration computed from log fields, by path
quantile_over_time(0.95,
  {app="api"} | json | unwrap duration_ms [5m]) by (path)
takeaways: Stream selector first, then line filters, then parsers and label filters
Only labels are indexed; keep high-cardinality values in the line
count_over_time, rate and unwrap turn logs into metrics and alerts
pitfalls: Putting `| json` before a line filter, so Loki parses every line instead of discarding most of them cheaply first.

quiz.q: Which query counts error lines per second for each app in prod?
quiz.explain: rate over a log selection in a range window, aggregated by app, is the LogQL metric-query form.

concepts.name: Tempo traces and TraceQL
concepts.summary: Find and read request traces in Tempo with TraceQL, the trace waterfall view and the service graph.
concepts.why: When a request is slow across five services, a trace shows which step took the time; metrics and logs can't.
concepts.body:
A **trace** records one request's whole journey through a system: say a web page asks the API, which asks the payments service and a database. Each step is a **span**, with a name, a start time, a duration and a parent span, so the spans form a tree. Spans carry **attributes**, named details such as `http.status_code` or `db.statement`, plus **resource** attributes saying which service made them (`service.name`).

Collecting traces like this is called **distributed tracing**. Applications send their spans using OpenTelemetry, and **Tempo** stores them cheaply as files in **object storage** (cloud file storage such as Amazon S3). It finds a trace directly by its trace ID, the code shared by all of its spans, and can search by attributes too.

In Explore the Tempo data source offers:

- **TraceQL** queries. `{ resource.service.name = "api" && span.http.status_code >= 500 }` selects traces containing a matching span; `duration > 2s` filters by span duration, `traceDuration` by the whole trace. Pipelines with `|` add things up: `{ ... } | count() > 3` for traces with more than three such spans, `| avg(duration) > 1s`. Structural operators find parent/child relations, for example `{ span.http.route = "/checkout" } >> { resource.service.name = "payments" }`. The **Search** tab builds these without typing.
- **TraceQL metrics** (`| rate()`, `| quantile_over_time(duration, .95)` by attributes) chart traces like metrics, when Tempo's metrics-generator (a part that computes metrics from incoming spans) is enabled.
- Paste a **trace ID** to open it directly.

The **trace view** is a waterfall: spans nested by parent, bars scaled to duration, with a minimap to zoom, span details (attributes, events, logs) on click, and a highlight of the chain of spans that decided the total time (the critical path). Long bars with nothing under them mean time spent inside that service; many short sibling bars mean lots of small calls that could be sent together in one go.

Tempo's metrics-generator can also derive **span metrics** and a **service graph** (one node per service, and lines between them showing request rate, error ratio and **latency**, the time requests take), shown in the Node graph visualization, so RED dashboards exist even for services that have no metrics instrumentation.
takeaways: Traces are trees of spans with attributes; resource.* identifies the service, span.* the operation
TraceQL filters spans with { } and adds them up with | count(), | avg()
The waterfall view shows where time goes; the service graph gives RED numbers per service
pitfalls: Searching without any service or attribute filter over a long range, which scans most of the trace store.

quiz.q: What does { resource.service.name = "api" && duration > 2s } return?
options: Traces whose total duration is over 2s
Traces containing a span of the api service that lasted over 2s
Only the slow spans, without their trace
An error, duration needs a unit in milliseconds
quiz.explain: A { } block matches spans; a trace is returned when it contains a span satisfying all conditions.

concepts.name: Correlating metrics, logs and traces
concepts.summary: Jump from a latency spike to the trace behind it and from a span to its logs with exemplars, derived fields, trace-to-logs links and split view.
concepts.why: During an incident you move from a spike in a graph to the log lines and the slow trace behind it; the link settings are what make that one click instead of copy-paste.
concepts.body:
Metrics, logs and traces each answer a different question; **correlations** are configured links that let you move between them in Explore and on dashboards without retyping identifiers. They all rely on **shared labels** (`service`, `namespace`, `pod`, `cluster`) being named the same across Prometheus, Loki and Tempo, and on applications writing the trace ID (the code shared by all spans of one trace) into their logs.

The main links, configured on the data sources:

- **Exemplars** (Prometheus data source, Exemplars section): an exemplar is the trace ID of one real request, stored next to a histogram sample; Prometheus keeps them when started with exemplar storage. Enable exemplars on a panel's query and they show as diamonds on latency graphs; the internal link maps the `trace_id` label to the Tempo data source, so one click opens the exact slow request.
- **Derived fields** (Loki data source): a regex such as `traceID=(\w+)` or a structured-metadata field becomes a link next to each log line, pointing to Tempo with the matched ID. Clicking a line's **Logs context** shows surrounding lines.
- **Trace to logs** (Tempo data source): a span's service and time range become a Loki query. Map tags (`service.name` to `app`), add a time shift before and after the span, and optionally filter by trace or span ID.
- **Trace to metrics**: prepared queries per span, for example the service's error ratio with `$__tags` substituted from span attributes. **Trace to profiles** does the same with Pyroscope, Grafana's store of profiles (records of where a program spends its time).
- **Correlations** (Administration, Plugins and data): generic links from any result field of one data source to a query in another, with regex transformations.

The working pattern in Explore: open the RED graph, hover an exemplar, open the trace in **split view**, pick the slow span, jump to its logs. On dashboards, data links to Explore give the same path from a panel. When a hop fails, it is almost always a label mismatch or a missing trace ID in the logs.
concepts.code:
# Prometheus data source -> Exemplars
#   Internal link: Tempo       Label name: trace_id
# Panel query with exemplars enabled:
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (
  rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="api"}[$__rate_interval])))

# Loki data source -> Derived fields
#   Name: TraceID   Regex: traceID=(\w+)   Internal link: Tempo   Query: ${__value.raw}
# Log line: level=error msg="timeout" traceID=4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736

# Tempo data source -> Trace to logs
#   Data source: Loki   Tags: service.name -> app   Span start -1m / end +1m
# Generated for a span of service "api":
{app="api"} |= "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736"

# Tempo -> Trace to metrics, query template using span tags
sum(rate(http_requests_total{$__tags, status=~"5.."}[5m]))
takeaways: Exemplars link graph points to traces; derived fields link log lines to traces
Trace to logs and trace to metrics turn a span into Loki and Prometheus queries by mapping tags
Shared label names and trace IDs in logs are what make the jumps work
pitfalls: Tempo's trace-to-logs tag mapping left at defaults, so the generated Loki query uses service.name as a label and returns nothing.

quiz.q: What is an exemplar?
options: A trace ID attached to a metric sample, linking a graph point to a trace
quiz.explain: Exemplars connect individual metric observations to the trace that produced them.

quiz.q: Clicking a Tempo span's logs button returns no lines. What is the most likely cause?
options: The trace-to-logs tag mapping doesn't match the Loki label names, or the log lines lack the trace ID
Exemplars are disabled on the Prometheus data source
quiz.explain: The generated query is built from mapped span tags; wrong label names or missing IDs select nothing.

concepts.name: Grafana Alerting overview
concepts.summary: Create alert rules with queries, expressions and pending periods, and route notifications through contact points and notification policies.
concepts.why: Dashboards only help when someone is looking; alert rules turn them into notifications.
concepts.body:
Grafana Alerting has three main parts, found under **Alerting**:

- **Alert rules**: one or more queries, then **expressions** that reduce and compare them, for example query A, **Reduce** to the last value, **Threshold** above 0.05. Rules are evaluated by an **evaluation group** on an interval, and have a **pending period**: the condition must hold that long before the alert fires, just like Prometheus's `for`. Rules can carry labels and annotations such as summary and runbook URL, and can be linked to a dashboard panel.
- **Contact points**: where notifications go: email, Slack, PagerDuty, Microsoft Teams, **webhooks** (an HTTP request Grafana sends to an address you choose) and more, with messages built from **templates**, text with blanks Grafana fills in.
- **Notification policies**: a tree that matches alert labels to contact points, with grouping, timing and nested policies, the same model as Prometheus Alertmanager. **Silences** and **mute timings** suppress notifications temporarily or on a schedule.

Grafana-managed rules can query **any** data source that runs its queries on the Grafana server (most do), including SQL databases, and combine several. Alternatively, rules for Prometheus (or Mimir, Grafana's large-scale store for Prometheus data) can be **data source-managed**: stored and checked by Prometheus itself and sent on by Alertmanager, with Grafana only editing them.

Each series returned by the query becomes its own **alert instance**, labelled by its labels, so one rule covers every instance. Configure **No data** and **Error** handling explicitly; the defaults decide whether a broken query pages you.
concepts.code:
# Grafana-managed alert rule (conceptual layout of the UI form)
# Query A (Prometheus):
sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
  / sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
# Expression B: Reduce   A  -> Last
# Expression C: Threshold B  -> Is above 0.05     (alert condition)
# Folder: Services  Evaluation group: api (every 1m)  Pending period: 5m
# Labels: severity=page team=api
# Annotations:
#   summary = Error ratio for {{ $labels.job }} is {{ humanizePercentage $values.B.Value }}
# Notification policy: team=api -> contact point "api-oncall" (PagerDuty)
# No data: Keep last state    Error: Alerting
takeaways: Rules = queries + Reduce/Threshold expressions + pending period
Contact points send; notification policies route by labels
Each returned series becomes a separate alert instance
pitfalls: Leaving No data handling at its default without thinking, so an exporter outage silently stops alerting or pages everyone.

quiz.q: How does a Grafana alert rule notify the right team?
options: Notification policies match the alert's labels to contact points
Each rule names an email address
quiz.explain: Routing is label-based through the notification policy tree.

concepts.name: Alert rule anatomy: queries and expressions
concepts.summary: Build a Grafana-managed rule step by step: queries, Reduce, Math and Threshold expressions, the condition, labels, templated annotations, pending period.
concepts.why: A rule is a small data pipeline; understanding each stage is what lets you answer "why did this fire?" and "why didn't it?".
concepts.body:
A **Grafana-managed alert rule** is built in the rule editor as a chain of **queries** and **expressions**, each with a letter (`A`, `B`, `C`), and exactly one of them is marked as the **alert condition**.

- **Queries** run against a data source, over a relative window such as the last 5 minutes. Each series returned becomes a separate **alert instance**, labelled with the series labels, so one rule covers every job, server or disk.
- **Reduce** turns each time series into a number: function Last, Mean, Min, Max, Sum, Count; mode Strict (the result is NaN, "not a number", if any point isn't a number), Replace non-numbers, or Drop non-numbers.
- **Math** evaluates an expression over earlier results: `$B > 0.05`, `$A / $C * 100`, `abs($A - $B)`. Series are matched by labels.
- **Threshold** compares with above, below, within range or outside range, and can define a **custom recovery threshold**, so an alert that fires above 90% resolves only below 80% instead of switching on and off around one value.
- **Classic condition** combines several queries into one instance, which loses the per-series labels; prefer the others.

The condition gives each instance 1 (fire) or 0 (don't fire). The **simplified** rule editor hides B and C behind "WHEN last() OF A IS ABOVE 0.05" and builds the same chain.

Then the rule gets a **folder** and **evaluation group** (which fixes the interval), a **pending period** such as 5m (the condition must stay true that long; 0 fires immediately) and in recent versions **keep firing for**, which holds a resolved alert for a while to avoid **flapping**: an alert switching on and off again and again, sending a notification each time.

**Labels** (`severity=page`, `team=api`, templates allowed) decide who gets notified. **Annotations** carry human text: `summary`, `description`, `runbook_url`, templated with `{{ $labels.job }}`, `{{ $values.B }}` or `{{ humanizePercentage $values.B.Value }}`. Link the rule to a **dashboard and panel** so notifications include a link, and use **Preview** to see instances before saving.
concepts.code:
# Query A (Prometheus, last 5m):
sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
  / sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
# Expression B: Reduce     input A, function Last, mode Strict
# Expression C: Threshold  input B, IS ABOVE 0.05,
#                          custom recovery threshold: below 0.02   <- alert condition

# Rule settings
# Folder: Services        Evaluation group: api-fast (every 1m)
# Pending period: 5m      Keep firing for: 2m
# Labels:      severity=page   team=api   service={{ $labels.job }}
# Annotations:
#   summary     = High error ratio for {{ $labels.job }}
#   description = {{ humanizePercentage $values.B.Value }} of requests failed over the last 5m
#   runbook_url = https://runbooks.example.com/api/error-ratio
# Dashboard: API overview   Panel: Error ratio
takeaways: Rule = queries + Reduce/Math/Threshold expressions; one is the alert condition
Every returned series becomes its own alert instance with its labels
Labels route, annotations explain; both can use {{ $labels }} and {{ $values }}
pitfalls: Using Classic condition out of habit and losing the per-instance labels the notification policy needs.

quiz.q: Query A returns 12 series, one per pod. How many alert instances can the rule produce?
options: Up to 12, one per pod, each with the pod's labels
None until a Classic condition is added
quiz.explain: Grafana evaluates the condition per series; each series is a separate labelled alert instance.

quiz.q: Which expression type lets an alert fire above 90% but resolve only below 80%?
options: Threshold with a custom recovery threshold
quiz.explain: The recovery threshold adds hysteresis so the instance doesn't flap around one value.

concepts.name: Contact points and notification policies
concepts.summary: Route alerts: contact point integrations and templates, the notification policy tree with matchers and grouping, timings, mute timings and silences.
concepts.why: Alerts are only as good as who receives them and when; where each alert goes decides whether a page is useful or noise.
concepts.body:
A **contact point** is a named destination with one or more **integrations**: email, Slack, Microsoft Teams, PagerDuty, Opsgenie, Discord, Telegram, webhook, OnCall, and others. Each has its own settings and a **Test** button that sends a sample alert.
